Koh Samui's cafés cluster in Bophut and Fisherman's Village, Chaweng, Lamai and Maenam, with a growing number of specialty roasters and laptop-friendly spaces, plus a Thai coffee stall on almost every corner. Expect about 40–60 THB for a Thai iced coffee from a stall, 60–100 THB at a chain or local café and 90–230 THB for a specialty latte in 2026. Most independent cafés open at 07:00–08:00, so for a 07:30 tour pickup, eat at your hotel or grab a 7-Eleven breakfast.

We name a café on this page only when we can confirm it is open and as described; café openings and closures on Samui move fast, and online lists are full of places that have changed hands. Instead of a long list of names, this guide tells you which streets to head for, what to order, what it should cost and how to find a good café yourself, with a short list of places we're sure of. For meals, see Koh Samui restaurants.

Cafés by area

Bophut and Fisherman's Village

Bophut's old shophouses and the lanes between the ring road and the beach have the best concentration of cafés on Samui: espresso bars, French-style bakeries, brunch cafés and beach-front spots where you can drink a flat white looking across to Koh Phangan. It is busiest from 09:00 to 11:00. On Friday evenings the beach road becomes the walking street, so cafés close early or switch to drinks. See Fisherman's Village.

Chaweng

Chaweng is the practical choice: chain coffee shops and air-conditioned cafés inside Central Samui (open about 10:00–22:00), breakfast cafés along Chaweng Beach Road for a full English or eggs Benedict, and Thai coffee stalls by Chaweng Lake. On a wet day in the monsoon, the mall is the dry option. See Chaweng and shopping on Samui.

Lamai

Lamai's long-stay community of fitness, Muay Thai and yoga people supports health cafés: smoothie bowls, cold-pressed juices, plant-based breakfasts and good coffee near the gyms. Prices are a little lower than in Bophut. See Lamai.

Maenam

Maenam is quiet, and its cafés suit people who want to sit with a book or a laptop. Several small specialty roasters and home-style cafés operate in the village and along the ring road, some opening only a few days a week, so check hours before you drive over. See Maenam.

West coast and Nathon

Nathon has Thai-style cafés and bakeries used by locals and ferry passengers, open from early morning. Further south along the west coast, independent cafés are few and far between, and most visitors drink coffee at their resort or stop at a café attached to an attraction. See Nathon.

Thai coffee and tea: what to order

  • Oliang: strong, dark iced coffee brewed through a cloth "sock" from beans roasted with grains and sometimes soybeans; sweet and black.
  • Kafae boran / kafae yen: old-style coffee with sweetened condensed and evaporated milk, over ice. Rich and very sweet.
  • Cha yen: the bright orange Thai iced tea with condensed milk.
  • Cha manao: iced black tea with lime, refreshing in the heat.
  • Coconut coffee: iced coffee with coconut milk or coconut water, a Samui favourite in an island of coconuts.
  • Asking for less sugar: say "wan noi" (a little sweet) or "mai wan" (not sweet). Standard Thai iced coffee is very sweet.

Street-stall Thai coffee costs about 40–60 THB and is often served in a plastic bag or cup with a straw; bring a reusable cup if you can.

Specialty coffee on Samui

Specialty coffee has arrived in force since the pandemic: single-origin pour-overs, cold brew and well-pulled espresso are easy to find in Bophut, Chaweng, Lamai and Maenam, and several cafés roast their own beans. Many use Thai beans. Thai arabica is grown in the northern highlands of Chiang Rai and Chiang Mai, and robusta in the southern provinces of Chumphon and Ranong, on the mainland across from Samui. We know of no commercial coffee farm open to visitors on Samui itself. [check] A specialty latte costs about 90–150 THB at most independent cafés, with upmarket cafés charging up to about 230 THB.

Breakfast before an early tour pickup

Most independent cafés open between 07:00 and 08:00, while our Ang Thong speedboat tour picks up between 07:30 and 08:30. Your options:

  • Hotel breakfast: most hotels serve from about 06:30–07:00. Ask for an early or boxed breakfast the night before.
  • 7-Eleven: open 24 hours, with toasties, yoghurt, bananas, iced coffee and water.
  • Thai breakfast stalls: from about 06:00 near markets: jok (rice porridge), patongko (fried dough) with sweet soy milk, and khanom jeen with curry.
  • On the boat: the Ang Thong day tour includes lunch, so a light breakfast is plenty, especially if you get seasick.

Ang Thong Marine Park is closed from 1 November to 15 December; in that window, the Pig Island speedboat tour runs every day and leaves from Thong Krut in the south, with pickup times sent the evening before.

Working from a café

Samui is popular with remote workers, and most cafés have free Wi-Fi. Speeds vary from excellent fibre to unusable, and power sockets are often scarce.

  • Ask first: some cafés limit laptops at busy brunch times or have laptop-free zones.
  • Order regularly: buy something every hour or two if you stay for a long session.
  • Back up your connection: a Thai SIM or eSIM with unlimited data costs about 1,199 THB for 30 days and works as a hotspot when café Wi-Fi drops. See SIM cards and Wi-Fi.
  • Power cuts: short outages happen in storms; save often.
  • Coworking: for calls and long days, a dedicated coworking space with a day pass is more reliable than a café. Several operate in Chaweng, Bophut and Lamai.
  • Visas: working remotely for an overseas employer on a long stay usually needs the right visa; see Thailand visa guide.

Brunch and cafés with a view

  • Beach-club brunches: Nikki Beach at Lipa Noi holds a Sunday brunch, and CLUB SEEN at Avani Chaweng has run a Sunday brunch. Book ahead and expect "++" prices. See beach clubs.
  • The Jungle Club: a hillside hotel restaurant and bar above Chaweng Noi with views over Chaweng Bay, open about 10:00–22:00; a coffee or breakfast with a view, reached by a very steep road. Take a taxi or their pick-up truck rather than a scooter.
  • Fisherman's Village beach front: morning coffee with Koh Phangan on the horizon.

Animal and theme cafés

A capybara café in Lamai has become a family favourite, with entry at about 400 THB for adults and 300 THB for children aged 3–12. We arrange a private van trip to the capybara café (3,000 THB per van for up to 5). Before visiting any animal café, look at how the animals are kept: space, shade, water and rest from handling. We don't recommend venues where animals are chained or used as photo props.

Most cafés take cards or Thai QR payments, but small cafés and stalls are often cash only.

How to find a good café yourself

  • Look for a proper espresso machine and a grinder on the counter, and beans for sale with a roast date.
  • Check recent photos and opening days: many small cafés close one or two days a week, and some open only in high season.
  • Ask your hotel or villa manager, and the people at your gym or yoga class: long-stayers know the best coffee.
  • Be ready for low-season closures from May to June and September to October.

Coffee, then the sea

For a slow morning followed by an afternoon on the water, the Pig Island sunset tour (1,550 THB adult) picks up in the early afternoon and includes dinner. If you'd rather learn to cook what you've been eating, our small-group Thai cooking class in a garden kitchen costs 2,000 THB per person. Hotel pickup is included from most areas of Koh Samui.
